description: Hi, fellow Earthlanders! 🚀 We're two third-year Software Engineering students (ML + research) tackling Flame in Freefall for NASA Space Apps Islamabad. We need a teammate with a physics or engineering background, ideally combustion, thermal/fluid dynamics or aerospace, to help us understand microgravity flames and sanity-check our models. Interested, or know someone? Message us!
summary: We developed Combustion Atlas, an AI-assisted web dashboard that turns NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) combustion research into practical fire-safety insight for future crew habitats. It gathers all 26 PSI combustion investigations and ranks them by how relevant they are to a chosen environment: a spacecraft, the ISS, a lunar or Martian base, a pressurized rover, a spacesuit, or fire safety on Earth. Users explore the investigations as an interactive 3D constellation, compare test conditions side by side, and ask a role-specific AI guide questions that are answered only from PSI data. The dashboard addresses the challenge by summarizing, ranking and interpreting the investigations, and by surfacing what researchers and engineers need: fuels, oxygen levels, pressures, airflow, variables and sensors. Most importantly, it reveals where the evidence runs out. Future lunar habitats are expected to run at 30% oxygen or more, yet no solid-material flight test in PSI exceeded 21% oxygen, and there is no partial-gravity combustion data. Making these gaps visible helps prioritize the research that will keep astronauts safe.
details:
Combustion Atlas brings together NASA PSI’s 26 combustion investigations: 20 flight experiments and 6 ground studies that reuse flight data. For each one we recorded its objectives, fuels, sample and burner sizes, oxygen concentration, pressure, airflow, what varied between tests, what stayed the same, the sensors used, and its fire-safety takeaway. Where PSI doesn’t state a value, the dashboard says so instead of guessing.

Users choose their role (professor, graduate student, undergraduate, aerospace researcher or aerospace engineer) and the environment they want to protect. Each investigation is rated on six fire-safety factors: material flammability, detection, suppression and extinction, relevance to elevated oxygen or low pressure, how realistic the fire was, and how useful the data is for modelling. The dashboard weights these factors for the chosen environment and re-ranks everything instantly. Users can also adjust the weights with sliders.

Key features:

3D constellation: investigations appear as stars grouped by the hardware they used (ACME, MDCA, the MSG flow duct, Saffire, smoke and aerosol). A star’s size shows its relevance.

Investigation cards and dossiers: an animated diagram of each experiment, plus an indicator showing whether it was tested at the habitat’s oxygen level.

Oxygen and pressure chart: every test plotted against crew atmospheres.

Gravity chart: shows that microgravity and normal-gravity data bracket the Moon and Mars, where no data exists yet.

Comparison table: pinned investigations side by side, with shared values highlighted.

Back to Earth: links the research to terrestrial spin-offs.

Role-based AI guide: cites PSI investigation IDs and can move around the dashboard for the user.

Guided tour, dark and light views, and touch support on phones.

Benefits and intended impact

Researchers, engineers and students get one clear entry point into scattered PSI records, without reading through every investigation. Engineers can see which experiments apply to the habitats they’re designing. Students and professors can find datasets for theses and coursework. Most importantly, the dashboard shows what we don’t yet know, such as how materials burn at the 30%+ oxygen levels planned for the Moon, and in partial gravity. We hope it helps steer future experiments, such as LUCI and FM2, and informs material-selection standards.

Tools and technologies

HTML, CSS and JavaScript

three.js for the 3D constellation

Canvas 2D and SVG for the charts, animated diagrams and artwork

Node.js and Express for the server, deployed as a Vercel serverless function

The Google Gemini API, through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, for the AI guide; the server keeps the key private and limits requests

The NASA PSI data repository for the data

GitHub for version control

Creativity

Instead of a flat table of results, the research is shown as a living star map, with an astronaut that marks investigations pinned for comparison. The visual style draws on thermal imaging and vintage NASA posters. Each experiment has an animated diagram: burning droplets shrink, flames spread across fabric, and smoke particles grow. Each user role gets its own AI persona and guided route.

Factors we considered

Accuracy: only PSI data is used, unknowns are labelled, and the AI is restricted to the catalog.

Different audiences: each role gets its own guide, and students get explanations of technical terms.

Easy to read: a calm layout, high-contrast text, and support for keyboard use and reduced motion.

Works everywhere: desktop, tablet and phone.

Responsible use of the AI service: rate limits and a private API key.

Honesty about scoring: the relevance weights are our editorial judgement, and users can adjust them.
